Mr Daniel Hughes
Consultant Colorectal Surgeon
Westbridge General Hospital
40 Hospital Road
Westbridge WB2 4RT

14 September 2026

Dear Mr Hughes,

Re: Mrs Margaret Carter, DOB 03/05/1958

I am writing to refer Mrs Carter, a 68-year-old retired teacher, for urgent assessment and colonoscopy, as I suspect colorectal cancer.

Mrs Carter presented on 2 September with a three-month change in bowel habit, with looser stools three to four times a day and intermittent dark red blood mixed with her stool. She has also lost 5 kg unintentionally and feels increasingly tired, but reports no abdominal pain.

On examination, she was pale. Her abdomen was soft and non-tender with no palpable masses, and rectal examination revealed no mass, although there was dark blood on the glove.

Blood tests on 9 September showed iron deficiency anaemia, with a haemoglobin of 94 g/L and a ferritin of 8 µg/L. Her faecal immunochemical test was positive at 180 µg/g. Renal and liver function were normal.

Her only significant medical history is hypertension, treated with ramipril. She has no known drug allergies and no family history of bowel cancer. I have started ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily.

Mrs Carter understands the reason for referral and, although anxious, is keen to proceed. Her husband will accompany her.

I would be grateful if you could see her under the urgent suspected cancer pathway.

Yours sincerely,

Doctor
General Practitioner, Riverside Medical Practice

15 Hill Street
Northfield NF3 8PL

21 September 2026

Dear Dr Brooks,

Re: Mr Ravi Patel, DOB 17/11/1949

I am writing to inform you that Mr Patel, a 76-year-old man with COPD, is being discharged today after treatment for right lower lobe pneumonia, and to request your follow-up.

Mr Patel was admitted on 16 September with three days of increasing breathlessness, a productive cough and fever. He was hypoxic, with oxygen saturations of 88% on air, and a chest X-ray confirmed right lower lobe consolidation. His CURB-65 score was 2.

He was treated with controlled oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and a five-day course of prednisolone. Because of his penicillin allergy, he received intravenous clarithromycin, followed by oral doxycycline, which he should complete on 22 September. His steroids raised his blood glucose to 14 mmol/L, but metformin alone was sufficient.

He has improved steadily and is now mobilising independently with a frame. His regular medication is unchanged, and he has been referred for pulmonary rehabilitation.

I would be grateful if you could review him in one week, including his blood glucose, and arrange a repeat chest X-ray in six weeks to confirm resolution. You may also wish to consider a rescue pack for future exacerbations.

Yours sincerely,

Doctor
Respiratory Ward, Northfield Hospital

Dear Dr Reed,

Re: Ms Anna Kowalczyk, DOB 04/03/1981

I am writing to let you know that Ms Kowalczyk, a 45-year-old accountant, is being discharged today following uterine artery embolisation for symptomatic fibroids, and to ask for your help with her follow-up.

Ms Kowalczyk had heavy menstrual bleeding and pelvic pressure caused by multiple fibroids, the largest measuring 8 cm. She chose embolisation rather than hysterectomy. On 22 September, both uterine arteries were embolised through the right femoral artery, without complications.

She had severe pelvic pain overnight, which was controlled with morphine, and a low-grade temperature, which is expected after this procedure. Her groin puncture site is healthy.

She has been discharged on regular paracetamol, ibuprofen for seven days and codeine as required, with senna. She should continue her iron supplement, and she has a fit note for two weeks.

She may experience pain, low-grade fever and vaginal discharge for up to two weeks. However, fever above 38 °C, offensive discharge or worsening pain could indicate infection, and she should then contact us urgently.

We will see her in six weeks and repeat her MRI at six months. I would be grateful if you could check her full blood count in three months.

Yours sincerely,

Doctor
Interventional Radiology, Kingsway University Hospital

Dear Ms Clarke,

Re: Mr Kevin O'Brien, DOB 21/07/1977

I am writing to refer Mr O'Brien, a 49-year-old taxi driver who has recently been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, for dietary assessment and advice on weight loss.

A routine blood test this month showed an HbA1c of 58 mmol/mol, which was confirmed on repeat testing. Mr O'Brien weighs 108 kg and has a BMI of 34. He also has hypertension, which is treated with ramipril, and early osteoarthritis of the knees, which limits his exercise.

His diet is currently a major concern. Because he works night shifts, his meals are irregular, and he eats takeaway food four to five times a week. In addition, he drinks about 1.5 litres of sugary drinks a day and eats little fruit or vegetables.

I have started metformin 500 mg once daily, which will be increased gradually, and he is on the waiting list for a diabetes education course.

Mr O'Brien is motivated to lose weight and avoid insulin, and his wife is supportive. I would be grateful if you could help him plan healthy meals around his shifts, with a target of losing 5–10% of his weight.

Yours sincerely,

Doctor
General Practitioner, Oakfield Surgery
